## What this document is

Every number in the manuscript's coverage, agreement, and alignment results is recomputed here
from the committed run outputs, so a reader can see exactly which files each figure comes from
and which conventions were applied. Nothing is read from a cached summary table that this
notebook does not also rebuild from the per-cell records.

The notebook is **read-only**: it never writes into `benchmarks/cmd_sonnet5/out_v3/`, which is
frozen (see `REPRODUCE.md`).

Three axes are computed, and they answer different questions. Keeping them apart matters,
because the same pair of methods looks very different on each:

| axis | unit | question |
|---|---|---|
| **sample** | a curated row | does the other method describe this sample at all? |
| **field** | a (study, schema field) pair | does the other method populate this field for this study? |
| **cell** | a (sample, field) pair | do the two methods agree on the value? |

Throughout, *manual* means the curated cMD table and *automatic* means MetaExtractor +
MetaHarmonizer. Neither is treated as ground truth: the counts are reported symmetrically, and
which side is right where they disagree is a separate adjudication question this notebook does
not settle.

### Rendering

Gold tables are resolved against a checkout of
[`waldronlab/curatedMetagenomicDataCuration`](https://github.com/waldronlab/curatedMetagenomicDataCuration),
exactly as `benchmarks/cmd_sonnet5/bench_paths.py` does:

```sh
CMD_CURATION_DIR=/path/to/curatedMetagenomicDataCuration quarto render manuscript_data.qmd
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(jsonlite); library(yaml); library(dplyr); library(tidyr)
  library(readr); library(purrr); library(tibble); library(stringr)
  library(ggplot2); library(knitr); library(DT)
})

BENCH    <- "benchmarks/cmd_sonnet5"
RUNS_DIR <- file.path(BENCH, "out_v3")
SCHEMA   <- file.path(BENCH, "cmd.clean.linkml.yaml")
MANIFEST <- file.path(BENCH, "manifest.json")

CURATION <- "~/Projects/cMD_architecture/curatedMetagenomicDataCuration"
# CURATION <- Sys.getenv("CMD_CURATION_DIR")
if (!nzchar(CURATION)) {
  stop("Set CMD_CURATION_DIR to a checkout of waldronlab/curatedMetagenomicDataCuration")
}

RUNS <- c("sonnet_r1", "sonnet_r2", "sonnet_r3", "haiku_r1", "haiku_r2", "haiku_r3")
model_of <- function(run) ifelse(str_starts(run, "sonnet"), "Sonnet 5", "Haiku 4.5")
```

## 1. Inputs

### 1.1 The target schema

Both methods aim at the same schema, so it bounds what either can populate. The field names come
from the committed LinkML file — the same file the extractor was run against.

```{r}
#| label: schema
schema_fields <- yaml::read_yaml(SCHEMA)$classes$CmdRecord$slots |> unlist()

# Identifier / provenance fields. `bench.py::META_FIELDS` — scored, but reported in a
# separate bucket from the scientific-content metric.
META_FIELDS <- c("study_name", "sample_id", "subject_id", "pmid",
                 "curator", "ncbi_accession", "host_species", "uncurated_metadata")

# Unit and bound companions of another field. These are not independent observations: a
# populated `age_unit` only exists because `age` was populated, so counting them as separate
# field-level discoveries would double-count. Excluded from the field axis, kept in the cell axis
# (where the scorer uses them to convert values before comparison).
DERIVED_FIELDS <- c("age_unit", "age_min", "age_max", "age_years",
                    "antibiotics_exclusion_period_unit", "biomarker_unit",
                    "disease_response_os_unit")

content_fields <- setdiff(schema_fields, c(META_FIELDS, DERIVED_FIELDS))

tibble(
  set = c("schema slots", "identifier / provenance", "unit & bound companions", "content fields"),
  n   = c(length(schema_fields), length(META_FIELDS), length(DERIVED_FIELDS), length(content_fields))
)
```

### 1.2 The ten studies

```{r}
#| label: manifest
manifest <- fromJSON(MANIFEST, simplifyDataFrame = TRUE) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(study, pmid, n_samples, gold_rel)

manifest |> select(study, pmid, n_samples)
```

### 1.3 The "not reported" convention

A slot present in the output but filled with a not-reported sentinel is **not** a populated
value. This matters more than it sounds: the extractor emits all `r length(schema_fields)` schema
slots in its study-level `fields` object regardless of what it found, most of them carrying
`"not_reported"`. Counting key presence instead of value presence inflates automatic coverage
roughly fourfold.

The predicate below reproduces `metaextractor.evaluation.is_not_reported`, including its
treatment of lists (an empty list is not-reported; a non-empty list is a value), plus `NA` for
R's TSV reader.

```{r}
#| label: not-reported
NR_TOKENS <- c("not_reported", "na", "n/a", "", "none", "null")

# A sample cell is a bare scalar; a study-level cell is an object carrying $value.
cell_value <- function(x) if (is.list(x) && "value" %in% names(x)) x[["value"]] else x

is_nr <- function(x) {
  x <- cell_value(x)
  if (is.null(x)) return(TRUE)
  if (is.list(x)) return(length(x) == 0L)
  if (length(x) == 0L) return(TRUE)
  if (length(x) > 1L)  return(FALSE)
  if (is.na(x))        return(TRUE)
  if (is.character(x)) return(tolower(trimws(x)) %in% NR_TOKENS)
  FALSE
}

is_nr_vec <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  is.na(x) | tolower(trimws(x)) %in% NR_TOKENS
}

# Demonstration on a real record.
demo <- fromJSON(file.path(RUNS_DIR, "sonnet_r1", "ContevilleLC_2019.json"),
                 simplifyVector = FALSE)
tibble(
  quantity = c("schema slots emitted in study-level `fields`",
               "of those, carrying a value",
               "distinct content fields populated on >= 1 sample"),
  n = c(length(demo$fields),
        sum(!map_lgl(demo$fields, is_nr)),
        length(intersect(content_fields,
                         unique(unlist(map(demo$samples,
                                           ~ names(keep(.x, \(c) !is_nr(c)))))))))
)
```

### 1.4 Loading gold and extracted records

```{r}
#| label: loaders
read_gold <- function(gold_rel) {
  read_tsv(file.path(CURATION, gold_rel),
           col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), na = character())
}

# Fields the curated table populates for at least one row of this study, and the columns it
# carries at all. The distinction is load-bearing in section 3.
gold_field_sets <- function(g) {
  cols <- intersect(names(g), schema_fields)
  list(populated = cols[map_lgl(cols, ~ any(!is_nr_vec(g[[.x]])))],
       columns   = names(g))
}

# Per-field sample counts for one extraction. A field populated only at study level appears with
# n_samples_with_value = 0; the extractor's fan-out rule decides whether it reaches sample rows.
ext_field_counts <- function(path) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    return(tibble(field = character(), n_with_value = integer(), n_samples = integer()))
  }
  d  <- fromJSON(path, simplifyVector = FALSE)
  sm <- compact(d$samples %||% list())
  hits <- unlist(map(sm, ~ names(keep(.x, \(c) !is_nr(c)))))
  counts <- if (length(hits)) {
    tb <- table(hits); set_names(as.integer(tb), names(tb))
  } else set_names(integer(0), character(0))
  study_only <- names(keep(d$fields %||% list(), \(c) !is_nr(c)))
  tibble(field = union(names(counts), study_only)) |>
    mutate(n_with_value = coalesce(unname(counts[field]), 0L),
           n_samples    = length(sm))
}
```

### 1.5 The per-cell records

`write_cells_tsv` emits one row per scored cell of the all-curated join, for each of the 60
(model x repeat x study) combinations.

```{r}
#| label: cells
cells <- map_dfr(RUNS, \(run) {
  list.files(file.path(RUNS_DIR, run), pattern = "\\.cells\\.tsv$", full.names = TRUE) |>
    map_dfr(\(p) read_tsv(p, col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) |>
              mutate(study = str_remove(basename(p), "\\.cells\\.tsv$"))) |>
    mutate(run = run)
}) |>
  mutate(model = model_of(run),
         is_content = !field %in% META_FIELDS)

cat(sprintf("%s cell rows across %d run x study files\n",
            format(nrow(cells), big.mark = ","),
            n_distinct(paste(cells$run, cells$study))))
```

## 2. Sample axis — which samples does each method describe?

### 2.1 One-to-one alignment by identifier

This is the alignment reported in manuscript §3.3. A curated row is *matched* when its
identifier tokens pick out exactly one extracted record that no other curated row claims;
*pooled* when they pick out several; *ambiguous* when duplicated keys are involved. Neither
pooled nor ambiguous is resolved by position. Extracted records with no curated row are split by
whether they carry an identifier at all — the ones that do are candidate automatic-only samples
(for example deposited runs outside the curated subset).

```{r}
#| label: sample-axis
summaries <- map(set_names(RUNS), \(r) fromJSON(file.path(RUNS_DIR, r, "summary.json"),
                                                simplifyVector = FALSE))

alignment <- imap_dfr(summaries, \(s, run) {
  map_dfr(s$per_study, \(st) {
    a <- st$alignment
    tibble(run = run, study = st$study,
           n_gold = a$n_gold, matched = a$matched,
           unmatched_gold = a$unmatched_gold,
           pooled_gold = a$pooled_gold, ambiguous_gold = a$ambiguous_gold,
           ext_only_with_key = a$unmatched_ext_with_key,
           ext_only_without_key = a$unmatched_ext_without_key)
  })
}) |> mutate(model = model_of(run), .after = run)

alignment |>
  group_by(model, run) |>
  summarise(across(c(n_gold, matched, unmatched_gold, pooled_gold, ambiguous_gold,
                     ext_only_with_key, ext_only_without_key), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pct_matched = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * matched / n_gold))
```

Read symmetrically: `matched` are samples both methods describe, `unmatched_gold` are
manual-only, and `ext_only_with_key` are automatic-only samples carrying an identifier. The
manuscript reports the matched counts as 284 in every Sonnet run and 214/284/284 for Haiku.

```{r}
#| label: sample-axis-check
stopifnot(
  alignment |> filter(model == "Sonnet 5") |> group_by(run) |>
    summarise(m = sum(matched)) |> pull(m) |> identical(c(284L, 284L, 284L)),
  alignment |> filter(model == "Haiku 4.5") |> group_by(run) |>
    summarise(m = sum(matched)) |> pull(m) |> identical(c(214L, 284L, 284L))
)
cat("matched-row counts reproduce manuscript section 3.3\n")
```

Per study, which studies contribute the matched rows:

```{r}
#| label: sample-axis-per-study
alignment |>
  select(run, study, n_gold, matched) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = run, values_from = matched) |>
  arrange(desc(n_gold))
```

### 2.2 Which identifier carried the match, and why `sample_id` usually cannot

Alignment is **deterministic string matching, not a model call.** `metaextractor.alignment`
imports only `re`, `dataclasses`, and `typing`: it makes no network request and asks no LLM to
judge whether two samples are the same. Each identifier cell is split on `[;,\s]+` into a token
set, not-reported tokens are dropped, and a gold row matches a record only when their token sets
intersect on exactly one record that no other gold row claims. Every candidate key is tried and
the one yielding the most one-to-one matches is used for the whole study; ties in the token space
become *pooled* or *ambiguous* rather than being resolved. So the LLM decides what each sample's
identifiers **are**; nothing downstream negotiates what they **mean**.

That makes the `ext_sample_id` and `gold_sample_id` columns of `cells.tsv` worth reading
carefully, because neither is the matching key — both are simply each side's own `sample_id`
value (`evaluation.py`, `CellResult`). They differ whenever a study matched on some *other* key,
so comparing them reports the identifier vocabularies of the two methods, not the quality of
the match.

```{r}
#| label: id-vocabularies
key_used <- imap_dfr(summaries, \(s, run) {
  map_dfr(s$per_study, \(st) tibble(run = run, study = st$study,
                                    key_used = st$alignment$key_used %||% "(no match)"))
})

# An unmatched gold row has no extracted record, so `ext_sample_id` is empty and readr reads it
# as NA. `nzchar(NA)` is TRUE, so the NAs must be excluded explicitly or they survive the filter
# and poison the comparison.
id_pairs <- cells |>
  filter(!is.na(ext_sample_id), !is.na(gold_sample_id),
         nzchar(ext_sample_id), nzchar(gold_sample_id)) |>
  distinct(run, study, ext_sample_id, gold_sample_id) |>
  mutate(same = ext_sample_id == gold_sample_id)
stopifnot(!any(is.na(id_pairs$same)))

id_summary <- key_used |>
  left_join(id_pairs |> group_by(run, study) |>
              summarise(pairs = n(), identical = sum(same), .groups = "drop"),
            by = c("run", "study")) |>
  mutate(across(c(pairs, identical), \(x) coalesce(x, 0L)),
         differ = pairs - identical)

id_summary |> filter(run == "sonnet_r1") |> select(-run)
```

The split is entirely determined by the key: where the match ran on `ncbi_accession` the two
`sample_id` values differ for *every* pair, and where it ran on `sample_id` they are identical by
construction. There is no partial case in any run.

```{r}
#| label: id-vocabularies-all-runs
id_summary |>
  group_by(key_used) |>
  summarise(`run x study cells` = n(), pairs = sum(pairs),
            identical = sum(identical), differ = sum(differ), .groups = "drop")
```

What the differing pairs actually look like — the extractor writes the archive BioSample
accession into `sample_id`, while the curation writes the study's own internal label:

```{r}
#| label: id-examples
id_pairs |>
  filter(run == "sonnet_r1") |>
  group_by(study) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(key_used |> filter(run == "sonnet_r1") |> select(study, key_used), by = "study") |>
  select(study, key_used, extractor = ext_sample_id, curated = gold_sample_id, same)
```

Two consequences. The two methods share a `sample_id` vocabulary in exactly one study of ten,
which is why alignment falls back to `ncbi_accession` elsewhere — and why FanY_2023 matches
nothing at all: its curated rows list up to four run accessions each, but no extracted record
carried an accession, so neither key has anything to intersect. And because `sample_id` is an
identifier field, these systematic mismatches are scored in the `META_FIELDS` bucket rather than
the content metric, so they do not move the headline F1. Reading a specific sample's cells means
joining on `key_used`, not on the `sample_id` columns.

## 3. Field axis — which fields does each method populate?

### 3.1 Why this is not visible in the scorer's output

The scored field set is the schema intersected with **that study's gold columns**
(`bench.py::build_field_map`):

```r
build_field_map <- function(gold_cols) intersect(schema_fields, gold_cols)  # mirrors bench.py:91
```

A schema field the curated table does not carry as a column is therefore dropped before
scoring: the extractor's values for it produce no cells, and in particular are never counted as
false positives. Only the narrower case — column present, every row blank — reaches the scorer
as FP. Section 3.3 quantifies how much falls in the gap.

### 3.2 The three-way split

```{r}
#| label: field-axis
field_axis <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(manifest)), \(i) {
  m  <- manifest[i, ]
  gs <- gold_field_sets(read_gold(m$gold_rel))
  gold_pop <- intersect(gs$populated, content_fields)

  map_dfr(RUNS, \(run) {
    fc <- ext_field_counts(file.path(RUNS_DIR, run, paste0(m$study, ".json")))
    ext_pop <- intersect(fc$field, content_fields)
    auto_only <- setdiff(ext_pop, gold_pop)
    tibble(
      run = run, study = m$study,
      both        = length(intersect(gold_pop, ext_pop)),
      manual_only = length(setdiff(gold_pop, ext_pop)),
      auto_only   = length(auto_only),
      # of the automatic-only fields, those the scorer cannot see at all
      auto_only_unscored = length(setdiff(ext_pop, gs$columns)),
      auto_only_fields   = list(fc |> filter(field %in% auto_only))
    )
  })
}) |> mutate(model = model_of(run), .after = run)

field_totals <- field_axis |>
  group_by(model, run) |>
  summarise(across(c(both, manual_only, auto_only, auto_only_unscored), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(manual_populated = both + manual_only,
         auto_populated   = both + auto_only,
         auto_only_share  = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * auto_only / auto_populated))

field_totals |>
  select(model, run, both, manual_only, auto_only, auto_only_unscored,
         manual_populated, auto_populated, auto_only_share)
```

Units are (study, field) pairs summed over the ten studies, out of
`r length(content_fields)` content fields x 10 studies = `r length(content_fields) * 10`
possible pairs.

### 3.3 One run in full

```{r}
#| label: field-axis-diagram
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.6
FOCUS <- "haiku_r1"
f <- field_totals |> filter(run == FOCUS)

seg <- tibble(
  segment = factor(c("manual only", "both", "automatic only"),
                   levels = c("manual only", "both", "automatic only")),
  n = c(f$manual_only, f$both, f$auto_only)
) |>
  mutate(end = cumsum(n), start = end - n, mid = (start + end) / 2)

brk <- tibble(
  label = c(sprintf("manual (curated): %d", f$manual_populated),
            sprintf("automatic (MetaExtractor): %d", f$auto_populated)),
  start = c(0, f$manual_only),
  end   = c(f$manual_only + f$both, sum(seg$n)),
  y     = c(1.85, -0.85)
) |> mutate(mid = (start + end) / 2)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = seg, aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = segment),
            colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = seg, aes(x = mid, y = 0.5, label = sprintf("%s\n%d", segment, n)),
            size = 3.6, lineheight = 1.1) +
  geom_segment(data = brk, aes(x = start, xend = end, y = y, yend = y), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(data = brk, aes(x = mid, y = y, label = label), vjust = -0.6, size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("manual only" = "#dce6f1", "both" = "#b8cfe6",
                               "automatic only" = "#f2d9c2"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1.6, 2.6), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "(study, field) pairs populated by at least one method",
       title = sprintf("%s: field-level coverage", FOCUS),
       subtitle = sprintf("%d of %d possible pairs populated; %d of the %d automatic-only pairs are never scored",
                          sum(seg$n), length(content_fields) * 10, f$auto_only_unscored, f$auto_only)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.title.position = "plot")
```

The two methods populate almost the same *number* of pairs, but overlap on well under half of
them. Note that "both" means both put something in the slot — not that they agree on the value.
Value agreement is section 4.

### 3.4 Which fields are automatic-only, and are they plausible?

Presence alone cannot distinguish a field the curation genuinely missed from a schema slot the
extractor filled speculatively. Two diagnostics help triage: how many of the six runs recover the
field (reproducibility), and what fraction of the study's samples carry a value (a field asserted
only at study level, never reaching a sample row, is the signature of a slot-fill).

```{r}
#| label: auto-only-fields
auto_only_detail <- field_axis |>
  select(run, study, auto_only_fields) |>
  unnest(auto_only_fields) |>
  group_by(field) |>
  summarise(n_studies = n_distinct(study),
            n_runs = n_distinct(run),
            mean_sample_coverage = mean(if_else(n_samples > 0, n_with_value / n_samples, NA_real_),
                                        na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(n_studies), desc(n_runs))

auto_only_detail |>
  mutate(runs = sprintf("%d/6", n_runs),
         mean_sample_coverage = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean_sample_coverage)) |>
  select(field, n_studies, runs, mean_sample_coverage)
```

```{r}
#| label: auto-only-triage
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(auto_only_detail,
       aes(x = mean_sample_coverage, y = n_runs, size = n_studies, label = field)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, colour = "#c0764a") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 2.9, max.overlaps = 30, seed = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(-0.05, 1.05)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6, limits = c(0.5, 6.5)) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 7), breaks = c(1, 3, 6, 10)) +
  labs(x = "mean fraction of the study's samples carrying a value",
       y = "runs recovering the field (of 6)", size = "studies",
       title = "Automatic-only fields: reproducible and sample-level, or study-level slot-fill?",
       subtitle = "Upper right = recovered by every run and reaching most samples. Left edge = asserted at study level only.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

Fields in the upper right are recovered by every run and reach nearly every sample — the
strongest candidates for genuine coverage the curation does not have. Fields on the left edge
never reach a sample row despite being asserted, and fields low on the y axis appear in only one
or two runs; both patterns are consistent with speculative slot-filling rather than extraction.
Deciding which is which requires reading the source article and is **not** settled here.

## 4. Cell axis — where both methods report, do they agree?

### 4.1 The same counts, read as coverage

The scorer's five decisions carry a direction — they name one side "gold". Relabelled
symmetrically they are a coverage table, with no assumption about which method is right:

| decision | symmetric reading |
|---|---|
| `TP_correct` + `TP_wrong` | both methods populated the cell |
| `FN` | manual only |
| `FP` | automatic only |
| `TN` | neither |

```{r}
#| label: cell-coverage
cell_counts <- cells |>
  filter(is_content) |>
  count(model, run, decision) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = decision, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

cell_coverage <- cell_counts |>
  transmute(model, run,
            both = TP_correct + TP_wrong,
            manual_only = FN,
            automatic_only = FP,
            neither = TN,
            populated = both + manual_only + automatic_only,
            both_share = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * both / populated),
            agreement_given_both = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * TP_correct / (TP_correct + TP_wrong)))

cell_coverage
```

`agreement_given_both` is deliberately conditioned on cells both methods populated. A
chance-corrected statistic over the full table would be dominated by cells neither method is
really deciding — `manual_only` outnumbers `both` by roughly five to one — and would describe
the sparsity of the curated table more than the behaviour of either method.

### 4.2 Reproducing the manuscript's precision, recall, and F1

The directional scores of §2.4 follow from the same counts, with the curated table as
reference. Reproducing them here confirms the per-cell records this notebook uses are the ones
Table 2 was computed from.

```{r}
#| label: prf
prf <- cell_counts |>
  transmute(model, run,
            precision = TP_correct / (TP_correct + TP_wrong + FP),
            recall    = TP_correct / (TP_correct + TP_wrong + FN),
            f1        = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall))

fmt_range <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f-%.3f]", median(x), min(x), max(x))

all_curated <- prf |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(precision = fmt_range(precision), recall = fmt_range(recall),
            f1 = fmt_range(f1), .groups = "drop")

all_curated
```

The matched join is not in `cells.tsv`; its counts come from each study's `conditional` block in
`summary.json`.

```{r}
#| label: prf-matched
matched <- imap_dfr(summaries, \(s, run) {
  cc <- map(s$per_study, \(st) st$conditional$content)
  tibble(run = run,
         tp_correct = sum(map_dbl(cc, "tp_correct")),
         tp_wrong   = sum(map_dbl(cc, "tp_wrong")),
         fn         = sum(map_dbl(cc, "fn")),
         fp         = sum(map_dbl(cc, "fp")))
}) |>
  mutate(model = model_of(run),
         precision = tp_correct / (tp_correct + tp_wrong + fp),
         recall    = tp_correct / (tp_correct + tp_wrong + fn),
         f1        = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(f1 = fmt_range(f1), .groups = "drop")

matched
```

### 4.3 Consistency checks against the frozen outputs

Two assertions. First, the per-cell rows aggregate to the content counts stored in each run's
`summary.json` — so the cell axis and the scorer agree cell for cell. Second, the recomputed F1
matches the values reported in manuscript Table 2.

```{r}
#| label: checks
from_summary <- imap_dfr(summaries, \(s, run) {
  cc <- map(s$per_study, \(st) st$end_to_end$content)
  tibble(run = run, tn = sum(map_dbl(cc, "tn")), tp_correct = sum(map_dbl(cc, "tp_correct")),
         tp_wrong = sum(map_dbl(cc, "tp_wrong")), fn = sum(map_dbl(cc, "fn")),
         fp = sum(map_dbl(cc, "fp")))
})

from_cells <- cell_counts |>
  transmute(run, tn = TN, tp_correct = TP_correct, tp_wrong = TP_wrong, fn = FN, fp = FP)

comparison <- inner_join(from_summary, from_cells, by = "run", suffix = c("_summary", "_cells"))
stopifnot(all(map_lgl(c("tn", "tp_correct", "tp_wrong", "fn", "fp"),
                      \(k) all(comparison[[paste0(k, "_summary")]] ==
                               comparison[[paste0(k, "_cells")]]))))
cat("cells.tsv aggregates to summary.json content counts for all 6 runs\n")

published <- tribble(
  ~model,      ~score,        ~value,
  "Sonnet 5",  "all curated", "0.203 [0.180-0.216]",
  "Haiku 4.5", "all curated", "0.193 [0.148-0.193]",
  "Sonnet 5",  "matched",     "0.514 [0.452-0.538]",
  "Haiku 4.5", "matched",     "0.475 [0.468-0.484]"
)

recomputed <- bind_rows(
  all_curated |> transmute(model, score = "all curated", recomputed = f1),
  matched     |> transmute(model, score = "matched",     recomputed = f1)
)

left_join(published, recomputed, by = c("model", "score")) |>
  mutate(agrees = value == recomputed) |>
  rename(manuscript = value)
```

## 5. The values themselves

The counts above say how often the two methods meet; this section shows *what they actually
said*. Every table here is browsable — use the search box to filter to a field, a study, or a
value you want to check.

### 5.1 Where they both reported and disagreed

One row per distinct value pair, pooled over the six runs, most frequent first. The harmonized
columns show what each side became after MetaHarmonizer; they are blank for fields with no
crosswalk (only `disease`, `body_site`, and `treatment` have one), which are compared as
surface strings.

```{r}
#| label: disagreements
disagreements <- cells |>
  filter(is_content, decision == "TP_wrong") |>
  group_by(field, manual = gold, automatic = extracted,
           manual_harmonized = gold_harmonized, automatic_harmonized = extracted_harmonized) |>
  summarise(cells = n(), studies = n_distinct(study),
            models = paste(sort(unique(model)), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(cells))

cat(sprintf("%s disagreeing cells collapse to %s distinct value pairs; the 10 most common pairs are %.0f%% of them\n",
            format(sum(disagreements$cells), big.mark = ","),
            format(nrow(disagreements), big.mark = ","),
            100 * sum(slice_max(disagreements, cells, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)$cells) /
              sum(disagreements$cells)))

DT::datatable(disagreements, rownames = FALSE, filter = "top",
              options = list(pageLength = 15, autoWidth = TRUE,
                             order = list(list(5, "desc"))))
```

The disagreements are far more concentrated than the raw cell count suggests, and the largest
groups are disagreements of *naming convention* or *granularity* rather than fact — a country
name against its ISO-3166 code, a curated platform enum against the specific instrument the
paper names, a kit's manufacturer against its product name. All of them fall in fields that
§2.4 compares as surface strings, so a difference of convention scores exactly like a difference
of fact:

```{r}
#| label: disagreement-top
disagreements |>
  slice_max(cells, n = 12, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(field, manual, automatic, cells, studies, models)
```

### 5.2 Why those fields were not standardized

Two different causes sit behind the surface-string comparisons above, and they call for
different fixes.

**No vocabulary exists.** `Harmonizer` discovers its fields from the crosswalk files present in
the run tree (`crosswalk.py`: `self.fields = ... glob("crosswalk_*.csv")`), and
`regen_crosswalks.py` builds exactly three — `disease`, `body_site`, `treatment`.
`Harmonizer.canonicalize()` returns the value untouched for any other field, so MetaHarmonizer
was never asked about `country`: `MDG` and `Madagascar` reach the comparison verbatim. Nor could
it have been asked — the schema's `country_enum` carries no permissible values, so the extractor
received no vocabulary either and is free to emit an ISO code, a country name, or
`Brazil:Amazon Forest`. The slot's description does declare an intent (values should be
descendants of NCIT:C25464), but no corpus was built from it.

**A vocabulary exists and was supplied, but the output does not conform.** `sequencing_platform`
and `dna_extraction_kit` *do* carry static enums, and the schema loader passes them to the
extractor. Their disagreements are therefore not a harmonization gap at all — they are the model
declining to use an enum it was given.

```{r}
#| label: enum-conformance
enum_values <- yaml::read_yaml(SCHEMA)$enums |>
  map(\(e) names(e$permissible_values %||% list())) |>
  keep(\(v) length(v) > 0)

slot_enum <- yaml::read_yaml(SCHEMA)$slots |>
  map_chr(\(sl) sl$range %||% NA_character_)

conformance <- cells |>
  filter(is_content, decision %in% c("TP_correct", "TP_wrong"), !is.na(extracted),
         nzchar(extracted)) |>
  mutate(enum = slot_enum[field]) |>
  filter(!is.na(enum), enum %in% names(enum_values)) |>
  group_by(field, enum) |>
  summarise(reported = n(),
            # the scorer compares strings after trimming and lowercasing, so test membership
            # the same way rather than requiring an exact-case match
            conforming = sum(map2_lgl(extracted, enum,
                                      \(v, e) tolower(trimws(v)) %in% tolower(enum_values[[e]]))),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(non_conforming = reported - conforming,
         pct_non_conforming = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * non_conforming / reported),
         enum_size = lengths(enum_values[enum]),
         harmonized = if_else(field %in% c("disease", "body_site", "treatment"),
                              "yes - recovered by crosswalk", "no")) |>
  arrange(desc(non_conforming))

conformance |> select(field, enum_size, reported, conforming, non_conforming,
                      pct_non_conforming, harmonized)
```

Non-conformance only becomes a scored disagreement where the field has no crosswalk. `body_site`
appears here with a high rate, but its values are compared as ontology codes, so an extracted
`stool` against a curated `feces` maps to the same UBERON concept and scores correct. For
`sequencing_platform` and `dna_extraction_kit` there is no such recovery: the surface string is
the comparison.

The values the extractor emitted instead, for the two largest:

```{r}
#| label: enum-non-conforming-values
cells |>
  filter(is_content, field %in% c("sequencing_platform", "dna_extraction_kit"),
         decision %in% c("TP_correct", "TP_wrong"), !is.na(extracted), nzchar(extracted)) |>
  mutate(enum = slot_enum[field],
         conforms = map2_lgl(extracted, enum,
                             \(v, e) tolower(trimws(v)) %in% tolower(enum_values[[e]]))) |>
  filter(!conforms) |>
  count(field, extracted, name = "cells") |>
  arrange(desc(cells)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

Note that not every disagreement in these fields is a conformance failure: `NorgenBiotek`
against `MoBio` is a disagreement about which kit the study used, with both values inside the
enum. Separating the two is what the adjudication step is for.

### 5.3 Where the disagreements concentrate

Which fields the disagreements concentrate in:

```{r}
#| label: disagreement-by-field
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
by_field <- cells |>
  filter(is_content, decision %in% c("TP_correct", "TP_wrong")) |>
  count(field, decision) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = decision, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(both = TP_correct + TP_wrong, agreement = TP_correct / both) |>
  filter(both >= 50) |>
  arrange(desc(both))

ggplot(by_field, aes(x = agreement, y = reorder(field, both), size = both)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "#4a6fa5") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 8)) +
  labs(x = "agreement where both reported", y = NULL, size = "cells",
       title = "Agreement by field, cells where both methods reported",
       subtitle = "Fields with at least 50 such cells, pooled over six runs") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

### 5.4 Where they both reported and agreed

Shown for calibration: what the scorer counts as a match, so the disagreements above can be read
against it.

```{r}
#| label: agreements
cells |>
  filter(is_content, decision == "TP_correct") |>
  count(field, manual = gold, automatic = extracted, name = "cells") |>
  arrange(desc(cells)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15)
```

### 5.5 What only the curation reported

The manual-only cells, as distinct curated values. This is the largest population in the
benchmark, and much of it reflects what retrieval never reached rather than what extraction got
wrong — `QinJ_2012` and `LiSS_2016` returned abstracts only, so every populated curated cell in
them lands here.

```{r}
#| label: manual-only-values
manual_only <- cells |>
  filter(is_content, decision == "FN") |>
  group_by(field, manual = gold) |>
  summarise(cells = n(), studies = n_distinct(study), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(cells))

DT::datatable(manual_only, rownames = FALSE, filter = "top",
              options = list(pageLength = 10, order = list(list(2, "desc"))))
```

### 5.6 What only the extractor reported, in a field the scorer can see

The entire automatic-only *cell* population — every such cell in all six runs, listed in full.
These are the cases where the curated table carries the column but leaves it blank.

```{r}
#| label: automatic-only-cells
cells |>
  filter(is_content, decision == "FP") |>
  select(model, run, study, sample = gold_sample_id, field, automatic = extracted)
```

### 5.7 What only the extractor reported, in a field the scorer cannot see

This is the population from section 3, and it does not appear in `cells.tsv` at all — these
fields are absent from the curated table's columns, so `build_field_map` drops them before
scoring. The values are read back out of the extraction JSONs.

`level` distinguishes a value asserted on sample rows from one asserted only at study level; a
study-level value that never reached a sample row is the slot-fill signature discussed in
section 3.4.

```{r}
#| label: automatic-only-field-values
as_text <- function(x) paste(as.character(unlist(cell_value(x))), collapse = "; ")

ext_field_values <- function(path, fields) {
  empty <- tibble(field = character(), value = character(), level = character())
  if (!file.exists(path) || !length(fields)) return(empty)
  d  <- fromJSON(path, simplifyVector = FALSE)
  sm <- compact(d$samples %||% list())
  samp <- map_dfr(sm, \(s) {
    k <- intersect(names(s), fields)
    k <- k[map_lgl(s[k], \(c) !is_nr(c))]
    if (!length(k)) return(tibble())
    tibble(field = k, value = map_chr(s[k], as_text), level = "sample")
  })
  fl <- d$fields %||% list()
  k  <- intersect(names(fl), fields)
  k  <- k[map_lgl(fl[k], \(c) !is_nr(c))]
  stud <- if (length(k)) tibble(field = k, value = map_chr(fl[k], as_text), level = "study") else tibble()
  bind_rows(samp, stud)
}

automatic_only_values <- field_axis |>
  transmute(run, study, fields = map(auto_only_fields, "field")) |>
  pmap_dfr(\(run, study, fields) {
    ext_field_values(file.path(RUNS_DIR, run, paste0(study, ".json")), fields) |>
      mutate(run = run, study = study)
  }) |>
  group_by(field, study, level, value) |>
  summarise(runs = n_distinct(run), records = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(field, study, desc(records))

DT::datatable(automatic_only_values, rownames = FALSE, filter = "top",
              options = list(pageLength = 15, order = list(list(4, "desc"))))
```

A concrete contrast between the two patterns — one field recovered by every run on nearly every
sample, and one asserted at study level and never propagated:

```{r}
#| label: automatic-only-contrast
automatic_only_values |>
  filter(field %in% c("location", "fmt_id")) |>
  arrange(field, study)
```

### 5.8 The ontology mapping, automatic terms and curated terms side by side

For the three harmonized fields, both sides' terms are mapped through the same OntologyMapper
corpora before comparison (§2.5). The crosswalks are stored with the run outputs, so the exact
term-to-code assignment behind every harmonized comparison can be read directly. Curated terms
appear here only where the curated row carried no `<field>_ontology_term_id` of its own — where
it did, the stored identifier is used and no mapping is needed.

```{r}
#| label: crosswalks
read_crosswalk <- function(path) {
  read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    transmute(term = query, mapped_to = match1,
              code = match1_code, score = match1_score, stage = stage)
}

crosswalks <- list.files(file.path(RUNS_DIR, "crosswalks"), full.names = TRUE) |>
  set_names(\(p) basename(p)) |>
  imap_dfr(\(p, nm) read_crosswalk(p) |>
             mutate(side  = if_else(str_detect(nm, "_gold_"), "curated", "automatic"),
                    field = nm |> str_remove("^crosswalk_(gold_)?") |> str_remove("\\.csv$")))

crosswalks |>
  group_by(field, side) |>
  summarise(terms = n(), mapped = sum(!is.na(code) & code != ""), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(mapped = sprintf("%d / %d", mapped, terms)) |>
  select(field, side, terms, mapped)
```

```{r}
#| label: crosswalk-terms
DT::datatable(crosswalks |> select(field, side, term, mapped_to, code, score, stage),
              rownames = FALSE, filter = "top",
              options = list(pageLength = 15))
```

Because the mapping has no similarity threshold, a closed corpus assigns every term to its
nearest concept; a term with no genuine counterpart is recorded as `Not Found` and compared as
its surface string instead. The `mapped` column above shows how often that happens on each side.

## 6. The three axes side by side

```{r}
#| label: three-axes
axis_summary <- bind_rows(
  alignment |> group_by(model, run) |>
    summarise(both = sum(matched), manual_only = sum(unmatched_gold + pooled_gold + ambiguous_gold),
              automatic_only = sum(ext_only_with_key), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(axis = "sample (curated rows)"),
  field_totals |> transmute(model, run, both, manual_only, automatic_only = auto_only,
                            axis = "field (study x field)"),
  cell_counts |> transmute(model, run, both = TP_correct + TP_wrong, manual_only = FN,
                           automatic_only = FP, axis = "cell (sample x field)")
) |>
  mutate(overlap = both / (both + manual_only + automatic_only)) |>
  select(axis, model, run, both, manual_only, automatic_only, overlap)

axis_summary |>
  mutate(overlap = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * overlap)) |>
  arrange(factor(axis, levels = c("sample (curated rows)", "field (study x field)",
                                  "cell (sample x field)")), run)
```

The overlap fraction falls sharply from the field axis to the cell axis: the two methods reach
for many of the same fields, describe a minority of the same samples, and populate a small
minority of the same cells. The automatic-only column is near-zero on the cell axis and
substantial on the field axis for the reason given in section 3.1 — most automatic-only content
sits in fields the scorer never opens.
